topic: The Geometric Mirror: Planar Graph Duality and Euler's Formula
target_audience: Undergraduate Discrete Mathematics students or advanced high school students

sections.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Canvas
sections.content: Introduce the fundamental components of a planar graph: Vertices (V), Edges (E), and Faces (F). Emphasize that a planar graph must be drawn such that no edges cross. Define the 'unbounded' outer face to ensure the math stays consistent.
sections.example: Visualizing a simple square map where four cities (Vertices) are connected by four roads (Edges), creating one enclosed field and one infinite exterior space (Faces: 2).

sections.title: The Constant Harmony: Euler's Characteristic Formula
sections.content: Present the formula V - E + F = 2. Explain that no matter how complex a connected planar graph becomes, this relationship is an invariant property. Use animation to add vertices and edges to show the formula balancing in real-time.
sections.example: Start with a single triangle (V=3, E=3, F=2). 3 - 3 + 2 = 2. Add a 'bridge' edge to a new vertex: V=4, E=4, F=2. 4 - 4 + 2 = 2. The balance is always maintained.

sections.title: The Dual Transformation: Building the Mirror Graph
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a 'Dual Graph' (G*). Step-by-step visual construction: 1. Place a new vertex in the center of every face (including the outer face). 2. For every edge in the original graph, draw a dual edge crossing it to connect the new vertices in the adjacent faces.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Spider-Bot' sitting in each room (Face) of a floor plan. To talk to a neighbor, the bots spin a web (Dual Edge) right through the middle of the wall (Original Edge).

sections.title: The Mathematical Symmetry: V-F Swapping
sections.content: Explore the deep connection between G and G*. Explain that the number of vertices in the Dual (V*) equals the number of faces in the Original (F), and the number of faces in the Dual (F*) equals the vertices in the Original (V). The edge count (E) remains identical.
sections.example: A Cube graph (V=8, E=12, F=6) morphs into its dual, an Octahedron graph (V=6, E=12, F=8). Observe how the 'points' of the cube become the 'spaces' of the octahedron.

sections.title: Application: Duality in Design and Problem Solving
sections.content: Summarize how duality allows us to solve complex problems by looking at the 'opposite' perspective. Mention its use in map coloring or circuit board design where 'islands' of space are just as important as the 'traces' of wires.
sections.example: Two characters, 'The Builder' and 'The Navigator'. The Builder designs a maze of hedges (Original Graph), while the Navigator maps the paths between them (Dual Graph). Solving the Navigator's path automatically solves the maze layout.
